title: Hana-Kimi: For You in Full Blossom
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: Mizuki Ashiya, a Japanese girl raised in the United States, idolizes high jumper Izumi Sano, who has stopped jumping. She cuts her hair, poses as a boy and enrolls at his all-boys school, Osaka Gakuen, where she becomes his roommate and tries to help him jump again while keeping her secret, which Sano soon discovers and quietly protects.
life_message: Cheerful persistence and loyal encouragement can help someone you care about recover what they lost.

content.note: Comedic scuffles and dorm rivalries; no serious violence reported.
Light angst around Sano's past and the secret being exposed.
Romance, cross-dressing comedy and 'compromising positions'; Nakatsu's crush raises orientation themes; MU lists an attempted rape (to verify).
Teen comedy banter; profanity not documented (to verify).
Sano stopped jumping for personal reasons; emotional angst noted by reviewers.
Mizuki deceives her school and enrolls in disguise; her parents do not know it is a boys' school (Wikipedia).
Many drama and anime adaptations; no in-story marketing.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Dorm rivalries are friendly competition, not honor feuds.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Mizuki bends school rules and parental knowledge to follow her own choice.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty centers on dorm and school friends rather than family.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Dorm heads exist, but friendships are largely peer-level.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Gender norms are bent and questioned; no religious frame.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Following one's heart and identity play drive the story.

folkways.japan: Single-sex boarding schools, dormitory loyalties and sports scholarships reflect Japanese school culture of the 1990s.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers discuss humor, angst and art, not messaging (Wikipedia reception summary).
delivery.note: Themes of gender and loyalty come through comedy and situations rather than argument.

winners_losers: Mizuki's persistence and loyalty win sympathy, and Sano's recovery is the payoff; there is no ideological villain.
